text: Hello everyone, welcome. Today I'll be showing you Muse Port. Before the hackathon, I built an open-source toolkit with the bare-bones tools for an agent to port code. It's a dependency here, but everything on top of it, I built this week.

Muse Port takes code that only runs on NVIDIA GPUs and makes it run on other GPUs and CPUs. That's the first step towards more open AI: leaner, cheaper, and able to run on anybody's machine. So why not use AI to do it?
First up: Karpathy's GPT-2 trainer, llm.c. It normally only runs on NVIDIA. With Meta's Muse model, it now runs on SYCL, the open standard behind oneAPI: on NVIDIA, AMD, and CPUs.
It should run on Intel GPUs as well.
And Muse is the one doing this. It reads the entire repo, every CUDA file and kernel.
It writes a plan, and then it ports each piece in a loop.
Every piece is graded by a hidden check that the agent never sees.
The big test was llm.c's production trainer: almost five thousand lines of CUDA, ported in one run.
The toolkit also lets the agent rent GPUs by itself, on Runpod and DigitalOcean, with a spending cap, and every machine is deleted when the test is done.
Muse then tuned its own port on those GPUs: from 36 times slower than CUDA, to about one and a half times on mid-range NVIDIA cards.
We tried another repo, llama2.cu, and it was ported in one run too.
Along the way, we found a bug in oneMath, the open math library behind oneAPI, and we submitted the fix upstream.
And every result is in a report built only from the evidence, failures included.
Next, I'd love access to Intel GPUs, to port even more. The most interesting part is the workflow: an agent that ports code, then tunes it on real hardware.
Doing this for more projects is a great route to find a way for AI to run on more than just NVIDIA cards. Thanks for watching!
